lmhead.title: Output layer
lmhead.body:
Turns the final vector into “one score for every word in the vocabulary”.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › FFN & output › Output layer
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Another big table: one row per word in the vocabulary.
  • Compare the last position’s vector with every row (multiply position by position and add up)
  • the better the match, the higher the score.
  • For example “good” 2.64, “bad” 0.70 (example values).

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization (some models simply share the same table with the embedding table).

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted so the correct answer’s score keeps rising and the other words’ scores fall relatively.

▶ What it does in use

Read-only; computes the score of every word in the vocabulary.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • The “what I want to say next” vector has to become “a score for every word in the vocabulary”.
  • The simplest way: give each word a row of numbers and take the dot product of the vector with every row — the more they point the same way, the higher the score.
  • One matrix multiplication scores all words at once.

✅ Why this works

  • Training pulls the correct word’s row towards the final vector and pulls the vector towards the correct word’s row, so “pointing the same way = this word should come next” is made true by training.
  • See the link below for details.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Dot-product scoring was chosen because it is simple, parallelizes well and has stable gradients — not because it is the only possible design.

logits.title: Scores (logits)
logits.body:
One raw score per candidate word, positive or negative, not yet a probability.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › FFN & output › Scores (logits)
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

For example: good 2.64, bad 0.70, cold 0.47, hot 0.34, great 0.00 (example values). The gaps between scores determine the gaps between probabilities.

🌱 Where it starts

Not a parameter; computed fresh every time = final vector × scoring table.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Not adjusted itself (it’s computed); training adjusts the scoring table and all the tables before it.

▶ What it does in use

Handed to softmax to turn into probabilities.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • Give “raw scores” first rather than probabilities directly: scores can be positive or negative and are just the result of one multiplication, the easiest thing to compute
  • “turning them into probabilities” is left to softmax as a separate step.

✅ Why this works

  • Only the gaps between scores matter (adding the same number to all scores leaves the probabilities unchanged), so the model only has to learn “who is how much higher than whom”.
  • Adjustments like temperature can also act directly on the scores.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.

prob.title: softmax: next-word probabilities
prob.body:
Turns scores into probabilities that add up to 100%.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › FFN & output › softmax: next-word probabilities
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • First make every score positive (e raised to the power of the score), then divide by the total.
  • The lead of high scores gets amplified.
  • The result might be: good 70%, bad 10%, cold 8%…

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed formula with no numbers to learn.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Not adjusted itself; but the training “penalty” (the loss) looks at how much probability the correct word gets here: the less it gets, the bigger the penalty.

▶ What it does in use

Computes the probability distribution and hands it to sampling. “Temperature” can make the distribution sharper or flatter.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • We need a way to split things up that is “all non-negative and adds up to 100%” while keeping the order of the scores.
  • Raising e to the power guarantees all values are positive
  • dividing by the total guarantees they add up to 1.

✅ Why this works

  • Combined with the cross-entropy loss, the gradient is very simple: how much each word’s score should change = predicted probability − correct answer (1 for the correct word, 0 for the others).
  • The more wrong the guess, the stronger the push
  • a correct guess barely moves
  • training is very stable.

⚠️ Limits / notes: softmax is a common and effective choice, not the only one.

w1.title: Big table 1 (expand)
w1.body:
Expands the vector into a longer list (typically about 4× as long).

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › FFN & output › Big table 1 (expand)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Each new number acts like a “feature detector” that checks whether some pattern is present, e.g. “is this about the weather?” (an analogy).

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted to learn to detect useful features.

▶ What it does in use

Read-only; one multiplication.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Expanding to a longer list (about 4×) amounts to preparing lots of “detectors”, each recognizing one pattern; the more detectors, the more patterns can be remembered and told apart.

✅ Why this works

Each detector’s reading = the dot product of the input vector with its row; the more aligned, the higher the reading, so “this word fits some pattern” gets detected.

⚠️ Limits / notes: A single detector often reacts to several unrelated patterns at once; it is not always “one detector, one concept”.

act.title: Filter switch (activation function)
act.body:
Decides which detectors are “on” and which are “off”.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › FFN & output › Filter switch (activation function)
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • The simplest version (ReLU): negatives become 0, positives are kept.
  • Smoother versions are common today (GELU, SwiGLU, etc.; SwiGLU also uses an extra table as a “gate”).
  • Without it, two tables multiplied in a row equal one table, and the model would be far less capable.

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed formula with no parameters (except SwiGLU’s extra table, which is also randomly initialized and trained).

🔧 How training adjusts it

The switch itself isn’t adjusted.

▶ What it does in use

Computed on the spot.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • Table multiplication is linear: two tables multiplied in a row still equal one table, and without non-linearity a hundred layers amount to just one.
  • The switch introduces a “bend”, letting the model express “output only when a condition holds”.

✅ Why this works

  • With non-linearity, a stack of layers can express very complex rules
  • the switch also keeps most detectors “off” for a given word, so each word only calls up the small relevant part of the knowledge.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Which switch is best (ReLU / GELU / SwiGLU) was mainly settled by comparing experiments.

w2.title: Big table 2 (compress)
w2.body:
Gathers the active features and compresses them back to the original length.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › FFN & output › Big table 2 (compress)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Each active detector “writes” a little of the information it stands for into the result, forming the word’s new idea, which is then added back to the original vector through the residual.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted.

▶ What it does in use

Read-only; one multiplication.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Active detectors need to write “what I found” back into the word vector; each column of the second table is “what to write” for the corresponding detector.

✅ Why this works

  • After compressing back to the original length, the result is added to the original vector through the residual.
  • The whole “expand–filter–compress” works like a giant “key → value” table: the rows of big table 1 act like “keys” (patterns to match) and the columns of big table 2 like “values” (information to write).

⚠️ Limits / notes: “Key–value memory” is a common interpretive lens in research, not a rigorous proof.
